title: Ox and self forgotten
hook: eighth picture: both ox and self forgotten, an empty circle
carry: let go of the seeker too

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh picture: home, the ox forgotten, the man resting in the sun. Your line: the ox forgotten.

Turn to the eighth picture and there's nothing on it. No herdsman, no ox, no hut, no field, no rope. Just a circle drawn in ink, with empty paper inside. For seven pictures you've followed a man and an animal through grass and mud and weather. Yesterday the ox dropped out of the frame and the man stayed. Now he's gone too. It can look as if a page went missing at the printer. It didn't.
screen: `NO HERDSMAN. NO OX.` → `JUST A CIRCLE OF INK.` → `NOTHING MISSING.`

segments.voice: First, both forgotten. The Chinese title says it directly: person and ox, both forgotten. The verse, in paraphrase, lists them as they go: whip, rope, person, ox, all gone into emptiness. Yesterday he let go of what he was chasing. Today he lets go of himself as the one who chased it. Second, no place to stand. The preface says he doesn't linger where there is awakening, and passes quickly by where there is none. It isn't that he vanished. There's just no fixed spot left to point at and say, there he is, the enlightened man. Third, no praise can reach it. The preface mentions birds bringing flowers, an old story of a hermit so holy that birds brought him offerings, and says that praise would mean nothing here. The verse adds: the sky is too vast for anyone to survey; a snowflake can't fall on a blazing furnace. Even the idea of being special melts. Fourth, a circle is whole. An empty frame could look like loss, but a circle is unbroken. In Japanese Zen, drawing a circle in one brushstroke, the enso, became its own practice, showing the mind at the moment of the stroke. The emptiness here isn't a blank where something used to be. It's the paper the whole story was drawn on, still here when the herdsman and the ox are gone.
screen: `PERSON AND OX, BOTH FORGOTTEN.` · `NO PLACE LEFT TO STAND.` · `NO PRAISE CAN REACH IT.` · `A CIRCLE IS WHOLE.` · then, large: `THE EMPTY CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: If there's paper and a pen nearby, draw a circle once, in one movement; if not, trace one slowly in the air with a finger. Don't fix it: wobbly is fine, it's yours. Then look at the inside, empty and missing nothing, and let breath and thoughts come and go inside it.
The empty circle. The eighth oxherding picture: ox and self both forgotten, a single circle with nothing inside, whole and unbroken. Today's word.
Your line: let go of the seeker too. Ox and self forgotten, nothing missing, and no one left keeping score. See you on the other side of the circle.

howItsDone: In Zen, the eighth oxherding picture is drawn as an empty circle, and in Japanese Zen the enso, a circle brushed in one stroke, is practiced and hung in temples and homes as an expression of the mind at that moment.
